questions.q: What does a named capture group like `(?P<status>\w+)` let you do that an unnamed group doesn't?
options: Match faster than an unnamed group
Retrieve that piece of the match with match.group("status") instead of counting parentheses to find the right index
Match case-insensitively by default
Skip the line entirely if it doesn't match
questions.explain: Naming a group with (?P<name>...) lets you pull that specific piece out later by name via match.group("name"), which is far more readable than tracking numbered groups by position.

questions.q: In the log pattern, why is the reason= portion wrapped in `(?: ...)?`
options: To make the regex run in a separate process
Because successful checkout lines don't include a reason= field at all, so that part of the line is optional
?: always marks the start of a regex
It converts the match to lowercase
questions.explain: The trailing ? makes that whole non-capturing group optional, since only failed-checkout lines include a reason= field -- successful lines don't have one to match.

questions.q: Why is collections.Counter a better fit than a plain dict for tallying log results?
options: Counter can only hold string keys
Incrementing a key that hasn't been seen before just works and defaults to zero, instead of raising a KeyError, and most_common() sorts the results
Counter automatically writes its contents to a file
A plain dict cannot store integers as values
questions.explain: A plain dict raises KeyError on counter[key] += 1 the first time a key appears. Counter treats missing keys as zero, and its most_common() method returns entries already sorted by count.

questions.q: Why does the lesson build a short written summary in addition to the raw Counter tallies?
options: Because Counter objects cannot be printed directly
A few readable sentences are more likely to actually get read during an on-call handoff than a dump of raw numbers
Written summaries run faster than printing a Counter
CSV files require a summary sentence before they can be opened
questions.explain: Raw counts are useful but easy to skim past. A short readable line like the failure rate and top reasons is far more likely to actually be read and acted on.

questions.q: Why does the CSV report open the file in append mode ("a") rather than write mode ("w")?
options: Append mode is required for any file ending in .csv
Write mode ("w") would overwrite the file each run, erasing every previous day's row; append mode adds a new row instead
Append mode makes the CSV load faster in a spreadsheet
There is no difference between the two modes for CSV files
questions.explain: "w" truncates the file before writing, which would destroy the history of previous days' reports. "a" opens the file and adds new content at the end, building a growing record over time.
